Itangazo Amerika yasohoye ku bijanye n'impembo y'amamiliyoni y'amadolari, yavuze ko ayo mahera azohabwa umuntu wese azotanga amakuru ajanye na porogarama ya nikleyere ya Irani, harimwo ayerekeye «ibibanza, ibikoresho n'abantu bafitaniye isano n'iyo porogarama».

Iryo tangazo ryavuze ko kuba Irani itubahiriza ivyo isabwa n'Urwego mpuzamakungu rujejwe inguvu za nikleyere (IAEA), mu bijanye n'amasezerano yo kugenzura ibikorwa vyayo vya nikleyere, vyatumye urwo rwego rutakaza ubushobozi bwo gukurikirana no kumenya neza uko Irani iriko irakora canke ingene ishingura ibice nyamukuru bikenerwa muri iyo porogarama, nk'imashini zitwa 'centrifuges'.

Izo mashini zirakenerwa mu gukora 'uranium' ihinguye kandi yongewe inguvu. Iyo 'uranium' ishobora gukoreshwa mu guhingura igitoro gikoreshwa mu vyuma bitanga inguvu za nikleyere (réacteurs), ariko kandi, iyo yongerejwe ubushobozi gushika ku rugero rwa 90% canke rurenga, irashobora gukoreshwa mu gukora ibirwanisho ruhonyanganda.

Hari haciye imisi bivugwa cane ko, inyuma y'amatora yo hagati mu kiringo, Amerika ishobora gusubira kugaba ibitero bikomeye kuri Irani. Ariko imbere y'ayo matora, Trump yari yabwiye abanyamakuru ko ata cihutirwa cotuma ivyo bikorwa.

Mu kiganiro yahaye Imboneshakure Fox News ku musi w'imbere y'amatora, uwo mukuru w'igihugu yavuze kandi ko Amerika «ishobora gukenera kugaba igitero ku kibanza citwa Pickaxe Mountain», ikibanza co munsi y'ubutaka gifitaniye isano na porogarama ya nikleyere ya Irani.

Trump yavuze ko ivyo «atari ikintu gikomeye» kandi ko vyoshobora gukorwa mw' «isaha imwe».

Uwo mukuru w'igihugu yari amaze gukangisha incuro nyinshi ko Amerika izotera ibisasu kuri ico kibanza co munsi y'ubutaka gikekwa ko gifitaniye isano na porogarama ya Irani ya nikleyere.

Ariko rero, Trump hamwe n'icegera ciwe JD Vance baremera ko abantu benshi muri Amerika badashigikiye intambara na Irani, kandi ko ivyo vyagize uruhara mu gutsindwa gukomeye kw'aba Républicains mu matora yo hagati mu kiringo aherutse kuba. Ivyo vyatumye hibazwa ko reta ya Amerika ishobora kuba itacipfuza kubandanya iyo ntambara.

Ku wa gatanu, Trump yashimangiye ko Irani ishaka cane guhagarika intambara imaze amezi umunani ihanganyemwo na Amerika, yerekana ingaruka iyo ntambara yagize ku butunzi bwa Tehran no ku gisirikare cayo.

Yagize ati: «Ubu turiko turaganira na bo. Barashaka cane gushika ku masezerano».

Ku wa kabiri, umuvugizi wa reta ya Qatar mu bijanye n'imigenderanire n'ayandi makungu yavuze ko impande zompi «ziriko zirihweza ivyiyumviro twazishikirije», yongerako ko bagifise icizere c'uko hazoshobora kwumvikanwa ku masezerano.

Abaserukira Irani mu biganiro bari baganiriye n'abahuza ku ciyumviro co gusubira kwugurura Umuhora wa Hormuz mu kiringo c'imisi ibiri, igihe Amerika izoba imaze kwemera ivyo Irani isaba.

Amerika na Irani vyari vyashitse ku masezerano y'intango yo guhagarika intambara no gusubira kwugurura uwo muhora muri Ruheshi (6), ariko ayo masezerano yahagaze inyuma y'indwi nkeya, igihe Irani yasubira kugaba ibitero ku bwato bwari mu mazi, Amerika na yo igasubira gushiraho ibihano vyo mu mazi kuri Irani.

Children were among the injured people seen being carried into a nearby hospital

Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say at least 33 people, including women and children, have been killed in air strikes by Saudi Arabia.

There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government in Yemen.

Live video footage on Al Masirah - a television station run by the Houthis - has shown rescuers pulling bodies out of the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.

The bodies of young children can be seen among those dug out from the ruins.

The television station has also shown a number of injured people being carried on stretchers to hospital.

Saba news agency, which is also run by the Houthis, said the attack was carried out by Saudi Arabia on Saturday. It added that 39 people had been injured.

The Saudis have led a coalition that has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.

The war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited as a result of the Iran war.

A truce began to fall apart when Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Sanaa - which is controlled by the Houthis - to prevent an Iranian plane landing there.

The Tehran-backed Houthis subsequently targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia, then began hitting Saudi ships that have been using the Red Sea off the coast of Yemen as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz.

Major fighting has since resumed in Yemen between the Houthis and forces fighting for the Saudi-backed government of Yemen.

On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province, which has been the focus of much of the recent fighting, is reported to have killed 30 people.

The Houthis accused the Saudis of carrying out the strike, while government forces accused the Houthis of having fired a missile at the site.

The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.

The Saudis have regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has fired multiple missiles at targets inside Saudi Arabia, including airports and oil facilities.

Hours before the strike that hit al-Shariyah, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh.

The Saudi Ministry of Energy later said the Aramco tower had been hit by falling shrapnel in what it said was an attempted attack.

The state-owned oil company's building suffered minor damage.

A Houthi leader, Mahdi al-Mashat, has vowed that the group will take revenge for the latest attacks in Yemen.

Perezida wa Israel yavuze ko agiye guha umukuru w'abatavuga rumwe na reta, Gadi Eisenkot, igikorwa co gushinga reta nshasha ihuriyemwo imigambwe itandukanye.

Isaac Herzog amaze imisi agirana ibiganiro n'imigambwe, inyuma y'uko ata ruhande na rumwe, haba urwa Eisenkot canke urwa Benjamin Netanyahu asanzwe ari umushikiranganji wa mbere, rushoboye kuronka ubwiganze mu nama nshingamateka ya Israel (Knesset), inyuma y'amatora yabaye mu ndwi iheze.

Eisenkot agiye guhabwa imisi 28 kugira agerageze gushinga reta nshasha, akaba ashobora kwongerwa iyindi 14.

Uwo yahoze ari umukuru w'igisirikare ca Israel yanditse ku rubuga rwa X ati: "Iki ni co gihe co gushinga reta y'ubumwe mu bihe bidasanzwe. Nzokora ibishoboka vyose kugira twerekane ko tubibereye."

Nta mugambwe n'umwe urigera utsinda amatora muri Israel ku buryo uronka ubwiganze mu nama nshingamateka. Ivyo bisigura ko reta zose zagiye zirashingwa muri ico gihugu ziba zigizwe n'imigambwe myinshi yagiye hamwe.

Umugambwe Likud w'umushikiranganji wa mbere Benjamin Netanyahu hamwe n'abo bacuditse bo mu ruhande rwa 'Extrême droite' n'abayahudi b'aba 'Ultra-orthodoxes', baronse intebe 53 kw'120 zigize inama nshingamateka ya Isreal.

Umugambwe Yashar wa Gadi Eisenkot uri hagati mu vya politike, hamwe n'iyindi migambwe itatu y'Abayahudi itavuga rumwe na reta iri mu runani rwiwe, baronse ibibanza 48.

Inani zibiri z'imigambwe iyobowe n'Abarabu, ari zo United Arab List na Joint List, zaronse ibibanza 19, ari vyo vyinshi cane vyambere iyo migambwe ironse mu mateka yayo, inyuma y'iyongerekana rikomeye ry'abatora mu Bayahudi b'Abarabu.

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Ivyo vyatumye izo nani zishobora kugira uruhara rukomeye mu guhitamwo uwuzoshobora gushinga reta. Ariko rero, imbere y'amatora, imigambwe yose y'Abayahudi, kiretse umwe, yari yiyemeje kutifatanya n'izo nani mu gushinga reta.

Herzog yavuze ko, inyuma yo kuganira n'imigambwe yose muri iyi ndwi, agiye guha Eisenkot akaryo ka mbere ko kugerageza gushinga reta.

Itangazo ryavuye mu biro vya Perezida wa Israel ryavuze ko yamenyesheje Eisenkot na Netanyahu ingingo yafashe.

Iryo tangazo ryavuze kandi ko, inyuma y'ibiganiro yagiranye n'intumwa z'abashingamateka bashasha batowe, Eisenkot yashigikiwe n'abashingamateka 67 ari we yokwemererwa gushinga reta, mu gihe Netanyahu yashigikiwe n'abashingamateka 46.

Perezida wa Israel arafise ububasha bwo kwihitiramwo umuntu abona ko ashobora kuronka imigambwe yomufasha gushinga reta. Nta tegeko rimusaba guha ico gikorwa umukuru w'umugambwe ufise intebe nyinshi kurusha iyindi mu nama nshingamateka.

Ivyavuye mu matora vyerekanye ko hari uburyo butatu bushoboka bwo gushinga reta: reta y'ubumwe irimwo imigambwe ya Netanyahu na Eisenkot; reta y'imigambwe yo ku ruhande rw'i buryo harimwo uwa Netanyahu hamwe n'aboshobora kwiyonkora kuri Eisenkot, canke gushinga reta iyobowe na Eisenkot, ishigikiwe n'imigambwe y'Abarabu.

Eisenkot hamwe n'abagize urunani rwiwe bose, kiretse umwe, bari baranse kwifatanya n'imigambwe y'Abarabu mu gushinga reta. Ariko hari abibaza ko hashobora kuboneka amasezerano yotuma bashobora gukorana.

Eisenkot ashobora kandi kugerageza kwumvikana n'imigambwe y'Abayahudi b'aba 'ultra-orthodoxes', ariko n'ivyo nyene ntivyoroshe.

Hariho akarorero k'aho reta y'ubumwe yigeze gushingwa. Mu 2020, inyuma y'amatora atatu aho vyari vyanse ko haboneka uwutsinze afise ubwiganze bukenewe bwo gushinga reta, Netanyahu hamwe n'uwo bahiganwa wo hagati mu vya politike, Benny Gantz, barumvikanye ku masezerano yo gusangira ubutegetsi, aho uburongozi bwagiye burahanahanwa hagati yabo bompi.

Mu gihe c'ibiganiro Herzog yagiranye n'imigambwe itandukanye, yari yavuze ko kugira ngo hirindwe ko haba ayandi matora no kugira ngo hashobore gushingwa reta itekanye, yiteze ko "imigambwe n'abayiserukira batahura ko, bivuye ku kuntu ibintu vyifashe ubu, atari amasezerano yose ashobora gushirwa mu ngiro."

Hagati ya 2019 na 2022, ikiringo cari kirangwamwo ukutumvikana gukomeye hagati y'imigambwe muri politike ya Israel, habaye amatora atanu atandukanye, kubera ko Netanyahu n'abo bahiganwa bagiye barananirwa incuro n'izindi kwumvikana kugira bakorane.

At least six people were killed and more than a dozen others injured when a gunman opened fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland.

Three bodies were found at his home when it was searched by police. Here is everything we know so far.

The attack began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's Main Market Square, the bustling central point of the city which is popular with tourists.

Police said a man drove into the square before beginning to fire "at random people from his car".

Footage shows scenes of panic as people fled, with the sound of gunfire clearly heard.

A passing tram was shot at during the apparently random attack, shattering windows but no passengers were injured.

People run for shelter as gunshots heard in Krakow

Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.

A 24-year-old man who was arrested died in hospital early on Monday, police said. The man had undergone surgery for a gunshot wound.

The Krakow branch of the National Public Prosecutor's Office in Poland has announced an investigation into what constitutes "a terrorist offence".

Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows the moment a police officer confronts the suspect on the ground before firing his weapon several times.

The officer then falls to the ground, apparently having been injured himself.

Moment police officer appears to shoot Krakow suspect

Shop windows in the square have signs of damage, seemingly from bullets, with glass shards scattered along the floor.

City officials have urged people who live in the city and tourists to stay away from the area while an investigation continues.

The suspect's car, found at the intersection of Dietla and Stradomska streets, was checked for possible explosive devices, police said, but none were found. Residents of nearby buildings had been evacuated while the operation was under way.

Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed in central Krakow. Four victims are Polish, while a British national and an Austrian woman were also killed.

Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three bodies - two women and one man - were found at the gunman's house when it was searched after the attack.

On Sunday, Polish police confirmed those three victims had been identified as the alleged gunman's 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and his sister, who was 21-years-old.

Sixteen people, including five foreigners, two police officers and the attacker, were taken to hospital. The interior ministry later said they were from Austria, the UK, Germany, Portugal and Russia.

Tusk later named the injured officers as Senior Constable Jakub Kulik and Senior Constable Artur Morański.

One of the police officers was described as being in a "very critical condition" by a Polish government minister after being shot three times while arresting the attacker. The officer is undergoing surgery, he added.

In an update on Sunday, police spokesperson Katarzyna Cislo told Radio Krakow two women who were sent to hospital following the incident had been released and the remaining individuals in Krakow's hospitals are in a stable condition.

She said this included the two police officers who were injured.

Polish authorities have not confirmed the names and ages of the other victims.

Police have identified the attacker as a 24-year-old Polish man who has been named as Michal Oksinski by local media.

He died in hospital early on Monday morning, police said.

The suspect was wearing "military-style attire" and had a military-grade weapon, according to a police spokesperson. However, authorities said he was not a soldier.

"Many pieces of weapons and ammunition were found in his vehicle", the spokesperson added.

Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.

Officials initially reported the gunman had apparently been inspired by "far-right ideologies", but have since said they are still investigating any possible motivation.

The gunman's home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city around 200km (125 miles) from Krakow, has been searched with support from counter-terrorism police.

The shooting happened in one of the largest medieval squares in Europe, a busy location which is also a popular tourist destination.

Jonathan Balshaw from Ipswich was there with his Polish girlfriend Dominika. The couple were outside St Mary's Basilica, in the corner of the square, when the shooting started.

Jonathan said: "We ran down the side of the church and through the side door and hid with several other people until the gunfire died down.

"A lot of shots were fired, more than 20 with it sounding like multiple different firearms - there were two distinctly different noises."

Caitlin Shasby from Newcastle was in Krakow with her friend Jon for a long weekend.

She said they heard shots from their hotel room but were not sure what was happening until their hotel rang them and told them to "stay in our rooms until further notice".

Two surgeons who were nearby rushed to help those hurt after the shooting stopped .

Speaking of his and his colleague's experience, Prof Michal Pędziwiatr told the BBC: "We saw the shooting attack. And what a surgeon can do in a situation like this?... We decided to help the victims as soon as possible.

"We rushed into the area where the shooting was and started our rescue, because there were no ambulances available, there were no professionals around."

After travelling to Krakow, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism...that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."

Krakow Mayor Łukasz Gibała signed an order declaring a period of mourning in the city which will last until Wednesday, 11 November.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "I'm shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Kraków today."

"My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added.

US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose described it as a "savage and murderous attack".

The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the shooting was "a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland".

President Volodymyr Zelensky of neighbouring Ukraine called the shooting "shocking."

"On behalf of the Ukrainian people, and personally, I extend my sincere condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims," he wrote on social media.

KIGALI — First Lady Mrs Jeannette Kagame joined a predominantly young audience at the Kigali Convention Centre on Saturday evening to watch a play that uses humour, personal memory and storytelling to revisit some of the most difficult chapters of Rwanda’s history.

The play, Carte d’Identité (Identity Card), was written and performed by Rwandan artist Diogène Ntarindwa, popularly known as Atome.

The performance explores Rwanda’s history through the experiences of a family shaped by displacement, exile and the search for identity.

At its centre is the story of Atome’s father, Philippe Niwemuto, whose experiences of leaving Rwanda and living in exile become a way of examining the country’s history and the choices made by a generation of Rwandans.

Ntarindwa performs different characters, using humour to tell a story that is also marked by loss, displacement and difficult memories.

The play moves between Rwanda, Burundi and what was then Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of Congo.

It begins with earlier chapters of Rwanda’s history before moving into the experiences of Ntarindwa’s family.

Atome recalls his father telling him that he should understand himself as Rwandan above everything else.

That message becomes particularly important in a story shaped by years spent outside Rwanda.

The play recounts how the family left Rwanda through the southern part of the country and headed towards Burundi.

During the journey, Ntarindwa’s father witnessed cattle that had been cut and were bleeding, with blood mixing with milk.

The experience, according to the story told in the play, became one of the moments that convinced his father to leave Rwanda with his wife.

The family later found itself in Zaire, where another conflict forced them to continue their journey on foot towards Burundi.

It was also where Atome was born and raised.

He recalls a childhood in which the family survived on simple foods, including cassava and porridge.

The memories are presented with humour, even though the experiences behind them are painful.

Atome uses the stage almost as a conversation with his late father, returning to memories of their life in Burundi and the experiences that shaped his understanding of Rwanda.

The story also explores the desire to return home.

Although life in Burundi had become familiar, the longing to return to Rwanda remained strong.

But the family faced a country whose authorities at the time did not want refugees returning, with the argument that Rwanda was already full.

These historical experiences are not presented as a conventional history lesson.

Instead, Ntarindwa turns them into a personal story.

He moves between characters, memories and moments of humour, allowing the audience to confront difficult history without losing the human dimension of the people who lived through it.

That combination of humour and painful memory was central to the performance.

The play attracted laughter and painful memories, all in one evening.

The play touches on exile, identity, personal and collective memory and the relationship between generations.

It also asks younger audiences to engage with a history that many of them know largely through the experiences of their parents and grandparents.

For a production built around memories of displacement, the presence of a predominantly young audience gave the performance an added dimension.

The younger generation was not simply watching a story about the past.

It was being invited into a conversation between generations about where Rwanda came from and how those experiences continue to shape the country.

Jeannette Kagame watched the performance alongside the audience.

After the performance, Ntarindwa thanked the First Lady for attending and recognized the production team and the audience.

The evening also underscored the role of theatre in preserving and transmitting memory.

Carte d’Identité does not tell Rwanda’s history through dates and political speeches alone.

It tells it through a father and son, a journey across borders, a family separated from home and a child growing up in exile while carrying the memory of a country he had not yet returned to.

Through humour, music, emotion and storytelling, Atome turns those memories into a conversation with an audience that includes a generation born after many of the events he recounts.

The result is a performance that connects Rwanda’s past with its present, while asking a simple but enduring question: what does it mean to belong to a country when history has taken you away from it?

Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.

The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.

But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.

The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".

Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy.

"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.

The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away.

It's too early to tell which faction will win. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.

The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.

Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.

But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.

The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.

That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.

Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff , replacing Susie Wiles.

The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.

With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle

One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.

Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.

But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency.

"There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist.

"But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."

The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.

The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.

Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.

Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.

The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.

Tuesday night saw Trump's Republicans lose in states they had comfortably held for decades

Democrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.

It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".

Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.

He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."

The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.

With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?

Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.

Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.

In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.

Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination.

"Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.

Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.

Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.

Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are seen as contenders for the 2028 nomination

Other rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.

In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.

Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.

Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.

His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race.

"It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said.

"But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."

Fire engulfed Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat in Bavaria last month

Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.

Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.

Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.

But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.

Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).

But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.

Adolf Hitler used the mountain retreat to welcome guests

Before it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.

Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.

Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.

Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.

Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.

In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.

Before it was burned down, the Kehlsteinhaus or Eagle's Nest had long been a tourist destination in Bavaria

Around 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.

Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.

The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.

Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat

Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history.

"It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.

That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler killed himself: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."

The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.

Police say the old Nazi retreat was largely destroyed by last month's fire

But Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.

Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus.

"We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.

Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed.

"We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.

Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".

After Hitler's downfall, US soldiers captured the mountain-top retreat and are seen relaxing here on 4 May 1945

Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.

Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question".

"I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.

Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era.

With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.

A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.

In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.

The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.

But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.

As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was finally released on Thursday, after years of rumours that Nintendo would remake the game - considered one of the best ever made.

IGN called it "the biggest game of the decade" in their review , external when it launched in 1998 on the N64, and it set the standard for 3D games.

A lot of the things we take for granted in modern games - such as riding a horse, fighting with a sword and shield, or locking on to enemies with the tap of a button - were pioneered or perfected in Ocarina of Time.

It received an almost perfect score from critics and, decades on, remains the highest-rated game in history on Metacritic, which aggregates reviews.

So how do you remake what many consider a masterpiece?

WATCH: Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time - how the remake compares to the original

Those like me who grew up playing the original will feel right at home here.

Nintendo has decided against reinventing the wheel, instead producing something which plays very similarly to the N64 classic.

As I've said before , video game remakes are a bit different to film or TV - gaming fans often clamour for a new take on their favourites, hoping developers harness evolution in tech to make them fresh.

And games have come a long way in the almost 30 years since the original Ocarina of Time came out.

"When you compare the games in the past and the games in modern times, so to speak, the norms of what people expect from a game have evolved naturally," Nintendo producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi told me.

"In the past, games where the users may have needed more imagination to fill the blanks or the gaps are now clearly expressed through the graphics that they see on the screen."

Even the most ardent critic would have to admit the game looks stunning

But fancy graphics have come at a price - a pivot away from realism into something a bit more cartoonish. Some might even be disappointed by this, given the N64 game had quite horrifying elements in places.

One was the Skulltula House, a room where people had been morphed into human-spider hybrids.

"Back when we created the original Ocarina of Time, the means to convey or express ideas was limited compared with what we have now," series producer Eiji Aonuma - who worked on the original game - said.

"With regard to even the so-called scary elements, we strove to add a touch of the comical."

But he told the BBC that enhanced graphics and lighting capabilities unintentionally exaggerated the already-spooky Skulltula House and its potential to strike fear into players.

"When we carried out the test play, the testers were telling us, 'Oh, this is too scary'," he said. "So of course, in the end product, we've made the necessary adjustments so that we can retain the same balance that we had achieved in the original."

I spoke to a few YouTubers about the upcoming game to get their thoughts - and the response was overwhelmingly positive.

Mike Channell, co-editor of the YouTube channel Outside Xbox, said he believed the remake had been made "very meticulously" in the hopes of living up to fan expectations.

"Having played the game, it's clear that serious thought has gone into every decision, to the point where I'm not convinced this remake has taken any less time and effort than an all-new Zelda game," he said.

"Ocarina of Time is obviously one of the great video game experiences in the history of the medium, but I have no doubt this new version will be the best way to experience this story.

"It's fleshed out as a world, sumptuously detailed, and the controls match 21st-Century expectations."

The characters are really expressive in the remake, thanks to the stylistic graphics

Ed King, known as Zeltik to his 893,000 followers on YouTube, said "the level of detail and charm" in the Ocarina of Time remake stood out.

"The Forest Temple has always been my favourite Zelda dungeon: a mysterious, haunted mansion in the deep woods, a lost work of man slowly being reclaimed by nature," he said. "The remake really leans into the surreal, uncanny nature of the original dungeon."

And fellow YouTuber StrawHatMidas said it was the "perfect" way to "bring this classic back".

"Not only does the game pay homage to the Nintendo 64 original, but it also expands on the things that made it so memorable," he said. "Everything from the world and atmosphere to the controls and soundtrack feels like a love letter to the classic Zelda formula."

Nintendo has made some big changes, not least to the Water Temple - a dungeon about two thirds into the game.

Aonuma said, having worked on the original, this was what he personally wanted to change most due to its reputation for being "very, very difficult".

He said there was now "a greater facility in tackling" the dungeon, as players can now easily change a critical in-game item known as heavy boots and have "the ability to leverage the camera orientation".

I grew up playing Zelda on the N64, which pioneered the joystick - but nowadays two sticks is the standard, with one to move and one to control the camera.

As far as I'm concerned, being able to freely move the camera this time round was a significant improvement.

Link's fingers now move over the holes of the ocarina as he plays

At times, the trip down memory lane was captivating. I knew where to go and what to do, thanks to a kind of muscle memory. However, on occasion that took away from the experience - with some tasks achieved too easily and some puzzles too quickly because I recalled their solutions.

Some people will love how similar it is, but I have to wonder if Nintendo has played things a bit too safe.

I don't think the developers see it that way.

"Even if the game may look different, we've maintained the essence that the original developers wanted to and hopefully conveyed through the original Ocarina of Time," Fujibayashi said.

Don't get me wrong - the game has lots of changes and surprises, and I won't spoil them, but I wish there had been more.

Then again, perhaps the best games leave you wanting more.

Or as Mike put it: "I loved the original as much as the next person, but I don't think I'll be going back to it."

Fans will no doubt wonder whether this is it, or if there will be more Zelda on the horizon. With the franchise's first movie coming next year, there's certainly more to come in the short term.

And in the long term, I wondered if with 30 more years of technological advancements, Nintendo might consider remaking the game once again.

"I will be long retired," Aonuma said, with a laugh.

Notts County beat Altrincham in incredible fog-filled spectacle

One of the most important attributes for a commentator is to be able to see the action you are trying to describe but that became a luxury for BBC Sport's Steve Bower when Altrincham hosted Notts County in an FA Cup tie on Saturday.

As thick fog enveloped the Moss Lane ground, he could barely see what was going on in a first-round game being televised live on BBC Two.

"One of the more challenging of my long career, that's about 35 years now," said Bower about the experience.

"I was reminded by a colleague - maybe I'm a jinx - that we had a similar thing on the BBC about three years ago when we did York against Wigan in the second round and the fog came in.

"Tonight was worse. From where we were, opposite the dugouts, once the play went to the centre circle and beyond, we couldn't see a thing.

"We couldn't see which team had the ball, let alone which player had the ball after about the 60th minute. Bearing in mind it went to extra-time, it was challenging.

"I just kept looking down at my phone and it was text message after text message from people saying, 'You're sounding great, but I can't see a thing'. In the end, you have to roll with it and do the best you can."

Notts County progress in FA Cup tie no-one could see

'It's like a fever dream' - commentators struggle through fog

National League Altrincham were on for an upset when they took a 2-1 lead against the League One side but a late Callum Roberts equaliser for County took the game to extra-time before the visiting side won on penalties.

"The frustrating thing is that for an hour it was a really good FA Cup tie, it had everything," said Bower.

"It was on for another giant-killing script but then the frustrating thing is that it becomes a non-event because, without stating the obvious, people can't see half of it.

"Also, it's not then about the tactics, or the shape of it, or the aggression, or the effort because you just can't see it. As a spectacle in trying to describe a game like you normally would, it's impossible."

Bower's radio colleagues were not faring much better as they tried to work out what was going on.

"I can just about see the bright white numbers on their shirts, but I am struggling to see what is happening on the far side of the pitch," said BBC Radio Nottingham commentator Adam Hassell.

Former Notts County striker Mark Stallard, who was also speaking on BBC Radio Nottingham, said: "We're looking around, and here in the press box no-one knows where the ball is! It's like a spot-the-ball competition.

"I played in the Notts County cup side against Wimbledon when it was abandoned - they equalised in the second half and I didn't see any of it!"

Stallard later said: "We genuinely cannot see the linesman or the players on the far side. It's slightly farcical having to commentate for radio listeners."

Altrincham have a rich history of causing FA Cup upsets but could not add to that in the fog against Notts County

The managers of both teams were on the touchline but even they were struggling as tactics went out of the window.

"[Notts County boss] Martin Paterson said credit to Altrincham, they were the better team in the first half and, as for the second, I couldn't see it. He was laughing," said Bower.

"Neil Gibson, the Altrincham manager, was saying, 'We were trying to get down to pitchside to look tactically at what they had done after those four substitutions. Have they changed shape? Is it a back four? Have they gone to a box midfield? But we just couldn't see'.

"So even from a tactical point of view, the players had to stop playing long diagonal passes and things like that because they couldn't see, they were just having to play short five, 10 yard passes so the game changed in that sense as well.

"It was very, very close to getting called off."

Bower said some of the players told him they couldn't see both goals or the corner flags from the centre circle.

"It will live long in the memory, that's for sure," said Bower. "Even on the penalties, you were having to rely on the crowd's reaction before committing to the tale.

"You couldn't see the goalkeeper's save, for instance, until the first replay came in."

The penalties took place in front of Altrincham fans and, while Bower had replays to call on, the Notts County fans "couldn't have seen anything" from the other end as they had to go on "crowd reaction".

"Obviously, the Altrincham fans all had their phones on with the lights trying to put the Notts County players off as well in the fog. A unique evening all around."

KIGALI – In Rwanda’s 30 districts, 182 international non-governmental organisations (INGOs) operate programmes covering healthcare, education, agriculture, poverty reduction, environmental protection and governance.

They work with communities, government institutions and local organisations, often implementing projects financed by foreign governments, international foundations, development agencies and their own headquarters.

Although their presence and activities vary from one district to another, the financial resources they manage are considerable.

During the 2024/25 financial year, the 182 international NGOs received approximately US$228.3 million in funding, following US$239.9 million recorded in the preceding financial year. Combined, the resources recorded over the two years amounted to approximately US$468.2 million.

Converted using the 2024 exchange rate, the combined amount is equivalent to roughly Rwf619 billion.

This is funding received by international NGOs alone. It does not represent the combined financial resources of all NGOs operating in Rwanda.

The figures raise an important question about the scale of international development financing in the country: after years of interventions and hundreds of millions of dollars channelled through international organisations, how much of that investment is producing visible and lasting improvements in the lives of Rwandans?

The figures are contained in the Government’s External Development Finance Report covering the 2023/24 and 2024/25 financial years, released in July this year.

Part of this government data examines development financing channelled through NGOs, including the resources received by international organisations operating in Rwanda.

The 182 international NGOs represent only a fraction of Rwanda’s wider civil society landscape.

A 2025 assessment by the Rwanda Governance Board (RGB) identified 1,487 local NGOs, 226 international NGOs and 76 foundations operating in the country.

The assessment therefore places the number of registered local and international NGOs at 1,713, alongside 76 foundations.

Local organisations account for the largest share of registered NGOs, but international organisations have access to substantial international funding networks that enable them to manage programmes worth millions of dollars.

The difference becomes particularly significant when their financing is examined.

The US$228.3 million recorded for 2024/25 translates into an average of approximately US$1.25 million per international NGO, if divided equally among the 182 organisations.

This is a mathematical average, not an indication that every organisation receives that amount. Funding is distributed unevenly, with some large international organisations managing considerably bigger programmes than others.

Nevertheless, the figures illustrate the financial weight of a relatively small group of organisations within Rwanda’s development landscape.

The resources also represent an important part of external development financing that is channelled outside the national budget and implemented through institutions other than government.

The sector distribution of funding provides an indication of the development priorities receiving the largest share of international NGO resources.

Social protection was the biggest recipient in 2023/24, accounting for US$92.4 million, or approximately 38.5% of the total.

Education followed with US$58.4 million, representing 24.3%, while health received US$36 million, equivalent to 15%.

Agriculture accounted for US$20.6 million, while governance and decentralisation received US$9.5 million.

The distribution changed considerably in 2024/25, although social protection retained its position as the largest area of funding.

Social protection funding declined from US$92.4 million to US$63 million, while education funding dropped from US$58.4 million to US$34.5 million.

Health, on the other hand, recorded an increase of approximately 20%, reaching US$43 million.

One of the most notable changes was in climate, environment and natural resources, where funding almost quadrupled from US$6.6 million to US$25.9 million.

Governance and decentralisation also recorded an increase, from US$9.5 million to US$14.8 million, while private sector development and youth employment rose from US$6.4 million to US$10.3 million.

The changing distribution suggests that international organisations are directing resources towards different priorities as development needs and donor interests evolve.

However, the amounts alone do not establish whether these interventions have achieved their intended results.

For instance, US$43 million in health funding does not tell us how many additional people accessed quality healthcare, whether maternal and child mortality declined as a result, or how much additional capacity was created in health facilities.

Similarly, US$63 million directed towards social protection does not establish how many households moved out of poverty or became economically independent.

International NGOs operating in Rwanda receive funding from several sources, including their international headquarters, bilateral development partners, multilateral institutions, United Nations agencies, foundations and other international organisations.

However, tracing the money to its original source remains a challenge.

In 2023/24, approximately US$130.6 million, representing 54.45% of the funding recorded, was attributed to multiple sources that were not individually disaggregated.

Another US$66.9 million, equivalent to 27.89%, was recorded as coming directly from the headquarters of international NGOs.

This means that more than 82% of the funding was either attributed to NGO headquarters or grouped under multiple sources without identifying individual contributors.

Funding recorded as coming from INGO headquarters increased to US$171.1 million, representing almost 75% of the total. Meanwhile, funding recorded under multiple, undisclosed sources declined to US$21.5 million, or 9.44%.

Other identifiable contributors included the Mastercard Foundation, which accounted for US$11.3 million, the United States with US$10.6 million, Sweden with US$4.3 million and Switzerland with US$2.4 million.

The report also identifies contributions from the European Union, Germany, the Netherlands, the Gates Foundation and other international partners.

The substantial reliance on headquarters financing is not necessarily unusual for international organisations, many of which raise resources globally before allocating them to country programmes.

However, the limited disaggregation makes it difficult to establish the complete financing chain: who originally provided the money, which organisation received it, which local partners participated and how much ultimately reached intended beneficiaries.

This is an important accountability issue, particularly when such substantial resources are being channelled through organisations operating outside the national budget.

Perhaps one of the most important questions raised by the scale of international NGO financing concerns the position of Rwandan organisations.

With 1,487 registered local NGOs compared with 226 international NGOs, local organisations constitute the overwhelming majority of the country’s NGO landscape.

Yet international organisations continue to manage substantially larger financial resources.

The External Development Finance Report’s analysis of financing channelled outside government provides another perspective.

National NGOs received 12.9% of the resources in 2023/24 and 11.9% in 2024/25.

International NGOs and private sector entities together accounted for 43.9% and 55.5%, respectively.

The report further notes that international NGOs received approximately twice as much funding as national NGOs.

These figures relate to the wider financing channelled outside government by development partners, rather than the total funding received by the 182 international NGOs in Chapter Six.

Nevertheless, they reveal a financing imbalance that deserves attention.

Local NGOs often have closer relationships with communities, understand local circumstances and have experience working with district authorities and grassroots institutions.

International organisations, meanwhile, often have access to larger donor networks, technical expertise and institutional capacity required to manage substantial grants.

This creates opportunities for partnerships, but also raises questions about whether international organisations are doing enough to strengthen local institutions.

Are Rwandan NGOs being developed into independent organisations capable of attracting and managing major development financing, or are they largely participating as implementing partners under international organisations?

There is also the question of how much of the funding benefits Rwanda’s economy through local employment, procurement, partnerships and the development of local expertise.

The available figures do not provide a sufficiently detailed breakdown to establish this.

The scale of this financing becomes even clearer when converted into local currency. Using Rwanda’s 2024 average exchange rate of Rwf1,322.7 to the US dollar, the US$239.9 million recorded for 2023/24 translates into approximately Rwf317.2 billion, while the US$228.3 million for 2024/25 is equivalent to about Rwf302 billion.

Together, the funding received by international NGOs over the two financial years amounted to approximately Rwf619.2 billion.

To put this into perspective, the Government allocated Rwf259.7 billion to agriculture in its entire 2024/25 national budget. The annual funding received by international NGOs was therefore equivalent to about 116% of that allocation, while the combined two-year amount was approximately 2.4 times the government’s agriculture budget for a single year.

In other words, the resources channelled to international NGOs over two years were enough to finance Rwanda’s entire annual agriculture allocation more than twice over.

The scale of international NGO financing makes accountability an important issue for the government.

Rwanda has been moving towards a more unified regulatory framework through Law No. 058/2024 Governing Non-Governmental Organizations, which came into force on July 19, 2024.

The legislation replaced separate laws that had governed domestic and international NGOs since 2012.

It introduced common requirements covering registration, institutional governance, financial management, reporting obligations and professional conduct.

Among its provisions, the law caps administrative and overhead expenditure at 20% of an organisation’s budget. NGOs must also maintain financial and institutional records for 10 years.

The law allows NGOs to conduct commercial activities, provided their commercial assets and operational assets are kept separate.

The Rwanda Governance Board, which regulates the sector, says the framework is intended to improve accountability, transparency and coordination between civil society organisations and government institutions.

The transition to the new framework has already attracted a significant response.

In a statement issued on July 30, 2026, RGB reported that approximately 86% of NGOs required to align their operations with the new law had submitted applications before the prescribed deadline.

The regulator attributed the response to nationwide awareness campaigns, training sessions, consultations and technical assistance provided to organisations.

However, RGB did not disclose the total number of organisations used to calculate the 86% compliance rate.

The 2025 registry figures provide a broader picture of the sector, although they should not automatically be used as the denominator for the compliance calculation.

The new law also provides an opportunity to establish a more reliable picture of organisations operating in Rwanda, their activities, financial resources and governance structures.

But registration and compliance alone do not demonstrate development performance.

An organisation can meet every legal requirement, submit financial statements and maintain proper governance structures without necessarily delivering significant improvements to the communities it serves.

Rwanda has made considerable progress in several development indicators over the past two decades, including poverty reduction, access to healthcare, education and social protection.

International NGOs have participated in many of these interventions, working alongside government institutions, local organisations and development partners.

However, attributing specific national achievements to NGO financing is not straightforward.

Many development programmes are jointly financed by government, bilateral donors, multilateral institutions and private foundations. Some involve several implementing organisations, making it difficult to isolate the contribution of a particular NGO.

This is where the latest financing report leaves an important gap.

It provides information about the resources received and the sectors attracting funding, but does not offer a consolidated assessment of the development outcomes attributable to the approximately US$468.2 million recorded over the two financial years.

How many people have moved out of poverty through NGO-supported programmes?

How many sustainable jobs have been created? How many farmers have increased their productivity? How many children have completed school because of these interventions? How many health facilities have improved their capacity to deliver services?

These are questions that should accompany annual funding reports.

The challenge is particularly important in social protection, which attracted US$155.4 million over the two financial years.

With such a substantial amount directed towards the sector, the public should be able to establish how many households benefited, whether their incomes improved and whether the support helped them become economically independent.

The same scrutiny should apply to agriculture, education, health and environmental programmes.

There is also the issue of sustainability.

Some organisations implement projects for several years, creating activities that depend heavily on continued donor financing. When funding ends, programmes may slow down or disappear.

A successful development intervention should ideally leave behind more than a completed project. It should create skills, infrastructure, stronger institutions, employment opportunities or economic activities that communities can sustain independently.

The ultimate test is not simply how many beneficiaries an organisation reports reaching, but whether their circumstances improve over time.

The 182 international NGOs operating in Rwanda represent an important development financing network. Their access to hundreds of millions of dollars annually provides resources that can complement government programmes and support communities in areas where additional investment is needed.

But the size of the funding also raises expectations about the results.

Rwanda has taken steps to strengthen oversight through the new NGO law. The next challenge should be to connect financial accountability with measurable development outcomes.

This could include requiring organisations to publish clearer annual reports showing funding received, project allocations, the number of beneficiaries reached, jobs created, local procurement, partnerships with national NGOs and independently verified results.

It would also help establish how much of the funding remains within Rwanda’s economy through local employment, procurement and partnerships, as opposed to expenditure on international operations and external expertise.

The disparity between international and national NGOs deserves particular attention. If local organisations are to become stronger development institutions, they need more than occasional subcontracting opportunities. They need access to financing, technical expertise and meaningful participation in programme design and implementation.

For RGB, the challenge is therefore not only to establish how many NGOs operate in Rwanda and whether they comply with the law, but also to ensure that the sector delivers value commensurate with the resources it receives.

Rwanda does not necessarily need more organisations or bigger development budgets. It needs development financing that produces lasting results.

After years of NGO interventions across the country’s 30 districts, the public should be able to see more than the number of organisations registered, projects launched or millions of dollars received.

The real measure of international NGO funding should not be how much money enters the sector every year, but how much that money changes the lives of Rwandans.

Abatora benshi bavuga ko ikibazo kibahanze kurusha ibindi ari izimba ry’ubuzima. Ibiciro vy’ibifungurwa n’igitoro vyaraduze, bivuye ahanini ku makori ari ku rugero rwo hejuru Trump yashize ku bidandazwa biva mu mahanga, hamwe n’intambara Amerika irimwo na Irani idashigikiwe na benshi. Ivyo rero ni vyo bija kuba biri mu mitwe y’abatari bake bagiye gutora. Ivyo birafasha gutahura igituma Trump ariko ariyamamariza no mu turere twahora dufatwa nk’aho aba Républicains badashobora kudutsindwa. Yongeyeko ati: "Amafaranga azokoreshwa mu kwiyamamaza muri Kansas azoba asumba na kure ayo aba Républicains bari biteze gukoresha." Ivyo vyerekana ko umugambwe wabo uriko uja muri aya matora ugerageza kwigwanira no kwigobotora. Mu myiyamamazo myinshi, Trump yateye akamo abanyagihugu abasaba kumutora. Mu kwezi guheze yagize ati: "Muri aya matora, ndabasavye mugire nk’aho ari izina ryanje riri ku rutonde rw’abitoza, ndabinginze.” Yongeyeko ati: “Mwishiremwo gusa ko ari ko biri." Yamara, ntari mu bitoza. MN202611_1ws8grn11vl.t: Gahunda y'Umuryango w'Abibumbye ishinzwe kubungabunga amahoro mu karere ka Sahara y'Iburengerazuba igiye guhagarikwa nyuma y'imyaka 35 ikorera muri ako gace. Ibi bije nyuma y'uko Akanama k'Umutekano ka ONU kananiwe kongera manda yayo, nk'uko Umunyamabanga Mukuru wa ONU yabitangaje ku cyumweru. Maroc, ivuga ko Sahara y'Iburengerazuba ari igice cyayo, yakiriye neza iki cyemezo. Gusa ku ruhande rwa Polisario Front, umutwe uharanira ubwigenge bw'ako karere ushyigikiwe na Algeria, bagaragaje impungenge zabo. Polisario Front imaze imyaka myinshi isaba ko Sahara y'Iburengerazuba iba igihugu cyigenga kuva ubwo Espagne, yari yarakolonije ako karere, yakavanagamo ubutegetsi mu 1976. Misiyo ya ONU izwi nka MINURSO yatangiye gukorera muri ako karere mu 1991, nyuma y'amasezerano yo guhagarika intambara yari yafashijwe kugerwaho n'Umuryango w'Abibumbye. Mu itangazo rye, Umunyamabanga Mukuru wa ONU Antonio Guterres yavuze ko tariki ya 1 Ugushyingo (11) ari bwo hatangiye icyiciro cyo gusesa iyi misiyo, aho ibikoresho n'umutungo byayo bizoherezwa mu bihugu byatanze ingabo zari ziyigize. Ihagarikwa rya MINURSO rije nyuma y'umwaka umwe Akanama k'Umutekano ka ONU kemeje umwanzuro wari washyigikiwe na Leta Zunze Ubumwe za Amerika, wemera gahunda ya Maroc yo guha Sahara y'Iburengerazuba ubwisanzure bushingiye ku kwigenga mu gihe ikomeza kuba munsi y'ubusugire bwa Maroc. ONU yari yarabonye iyo gahunda nk'igisubizo gishoboka kurusha ibindi mu guhosha uwo mwuka w'amakimbirane. Uburusiya, bwari bwarifashe mu gutora uwo mwanzuro umwaka ushize, uyu mwaka bwakoresheje uburenganzira bwo kuwutambamira, ku wundi mwanzuro wari ushyigikiwe na Amerika. Uwo mwanzuro wari gukomeza gushyigikira gahunda ya Maroc ndetse ukagabanya ibikorwa by'ingabo za MINURSO. Nyuma yaho, Akanama k'Umutekano kanze n'umwanzuro wari watanzwe n'Uburusiya, bituma manda ya MINURSO irangira nta yindi nshya yemejwe. Uretse kugenzura iyubahirizwa ry'amasezerano yo guhagarika imirwano, MINURSO yari ifite n'inshingano zo gutegura amatora ya kamarampaka yagombaga guha abaturage amahitamo ku hazaza h'ako karere. Ariko ayo matora ntiyigeze aba kubera kutumvikana ku bagombaga kugira uburenganzira bwo gutora. Minisitiri w'Ububanyi n'Amahanga wa Maroc, Nasser Bourita, yabwiye ibitangazamakuru bya Leta ko igitekerezo cya kamarampaka cyakomeje kuvugwa muri MINURSO ari "igisigaratongo cy'ibihe byashize kitagihuye n'ukuri kw'iki gihe". Yavuze kandi ko Maroc yari yamenyeshejwe mbere ko Uburusiya bwari bugiye kuburizamo umwanzuro wa Amerika, ariko ko Rabat yabibonye nk'"amahirwe yo gusubiramo bimwe mu byari bisanzwe bigenga iki kibazo." Ingoro y'Umwami wa Maroc yatangaje ko kutavugururwa kwa manda ya MINURSO ari "intambwe ikomeye" ishobora gutuma ikibazo cya Sahara y'Iburengerazuba kigenda kivanwa mu biri kwigwaho n'Akanama k'Umutekano ka ONU. Ku ruhande rwa Algeria, Minisiteri y'Ububanyi n'Amahanga yatangaje ku wa gatandatu ko yababajwe cyane n'icyemezo cyo kutongera manda ya MINURSO, ishinja Leta Zunze Ubumwe za Amerika kubogamira cyane kuri Maroc muri iki kibazo.
